title: Coti:
title_q: “I Told Them I Was Coming Back to Prison”
headline: He met MHA while he was incarcerated. Now he goes back into prison by choice, to help the men still inside.
story: Coti took WRAP while he was incarcerated. That is how he met MHA. Today he works for MHA in Omaha, and he goes back into the prisons to run WRAP groups. “I told them I was coming back to prison.”
This is the client's whole idea in one man: lived experience is what makes peer support different. It must feel proud and hopeful, never dark. It ends on four words: “Hope looks like tomorrow.”

Keep the room dark and warm. Lift his face a little only.
Hold 1 second on his face after “Hope looks like tomorrow.”
dont: No logo, name or title card at 0:00.
Nothing about why he was in prison. No crime, no sentence.
No OCC B-roll until Nick confirms the releases. No faces of the men inside.
Do not use 04:28–05:02 (WRAP for organizations). It belongs to the WRAP video.

transcript:
Auto-transcript of 20260910_C4824.MP4 (Coti, Terrapin Station, Omaha, 10 Sep 2026). Times are mm:ss in the source file. Speaker labels removed: they were all wrong. The interviewer is off camera.
[00:00] (Interviewer) Okay, I'll have you start with your name, your position.
[00:12] My name is Cody Khan. (transcript spelling; the folder says Coti. Not confirmed.)
[00:14] I'm property maintenance professional, peer support.
[00:24] I'm an intentional peer supporter and a wrap facilitator.
[00:29] (Interviewer) How did you first come across MHA?
[00:33] I was introduced to MHA while I was incarcerated.
[00:38] I took the Wellness Recovery Action Plan, and that's how I was first introduced to them.
[00:45] (Interviewer) What makes peer support different than traditional support?
[00:50] Peer support is moving through situations with somebody else.
[00:58] It's not being told how to do it.
[01:01] It's actually coming together and collaborating with somebody and figuring out your own way through it.
[01:08] (Interviewer) So tell me a moment that you still think about from a memory of MHA, either working there or being a participant.
[01:18] Well, even just like today, you know, I'm a wrap facilitator and it keeps coming up, reoccurring in these groups that I'm participating in.
[01:32] And a guy told me today, he said, you know, there's a lot of programming being, we're allowed to have a lot of programming and being incarcerated.
[01:49] He said, but this program right here, the wrap program, he's like, it's real.
[01:54] I keep coming back to it.
[01:56] And it's the only place I feel safe and vulnerable.
[01:59] And I have these conversations with these individuals inside all the time about the space that we create for them to be vulnerable and how comfortable they feel.
[02:09] So I mean, that's probably about the best, the best memories I got about this.
[02:14] (Interviewer) What would you say to someone who doesn't believe that they can recover?
[02:22] I've been there and I understand.
[02:25] It takes a lot of hard work and some time, but give it a chance, believe in it and believe in yourself.
[02:34] And it's possible.
[02:37] (Interviewer) What do people get wrong about this job?
[02:42] Like outside people or us, yes, absolutely.
[02:48] That's probably what it is too.
[02:51] Like the level of commitment from our staff, the understanding and the empathy that our staff carry with them to allow them to assist individuals in their journey, I think is really underestimated by outside people looking in.
[03:10] (Interviewer) If someone watching has never heard of MHA, what should they know?
[03:17] They're amazing.
[03:20] I've had a lot of people in my life, a lot of groups in my life give up on me and MHA's resilience and stamina to stick next to somebody through their hard times is extremely underestimated.
[03:37] (Interviewer) How has RAP impacted your life? What have you learned through RAP that you still use today?
[03:44] My RAP program is essential to my success.
[03:49] I learned everything about myself starting with RAP.
[03:54] It was the basis of everything I built today.
[03:57] So I actually learned how to be in touch with myself, learned what my emotions was, learned how I was feeling when I was feeling it from RAP.
[04:08] So yeah, it's the basis of everything I am today.
[04:13] (Interviewer) So we're trying to promote RAP to other organizations. So how does RAP benefit our organization? How does it trickle down to our participants and our culture so that we can encourage other organizations to also?
[04:29] So RAP is about communication.
[04:35] It's about knowing who we are and what we want.
[04:39] It's about advocating for ourselves.
[04:42] And it's about what we need, right?
[04:45] And to build any type of organization or any type of team within an organization, you need those things.
[04:54] You need to be able to communicate.
[04:55] You need to be able to know what you want, where you want to go, how you need it.
[05:02] And you need that.
[05:05] (Interviewer) I'm going to have you say, my name is Koti, and I'm a peer at MHA.
[05:11] My name is Koti, and I'm a peer at MHA.
[05:15] (Crew talk about his job title, 05:15–05:27.)
[05:28] (Interviewer) And then hope looks like blank.
[05:33] Hope looks like tomorrow.
[05:34] Oh, was I supposed to say that?
[05:38] (Interviewer) No, you're OK. No, that's good. I was just making sure you were done.
[05:40] (Interviewer) And then peer support is powerful because?
[05:44] Peer support is powerful because of the relationships we build within it.
[05:50] (Interviewer) One other question that I have for you, just from being inside the facility earlier today, one guy who was in the group we talked to, he actually brought you up by name and said you were a great resource and support for him. So as someone who has gone through peer support yourself, what does that mean to you to have other people saying that you were such a big help for them?
[06:24] It's pretty powerful, man, knowing the journey that I've been on and what I went through.
[06:30] And to be able to stand here today and reach my hand behind me and pull these guys along with me, it means the world to me, man.
[06:40] It's a proud moment when I hear these stories about guys inside still talking about the work I did inside of there and not knowing what I'm doing out here.
[06:50] But one day they will.
[06:52] I told them I was coming back to prison, you know, and I'm going back to prison and I'm going to keep on going back and trying to help them the best I can.
[06:59] So it's extremely proud moments for me.
[07:03] (Crew) I bet. That's amazing, man. Great answer. ... That's the best interview we've done all day.
[07:11] Give me a hug. I met you in there.
